title: The Closest Planet to the Sun Isn't the Hottest
hook_line: The closest planet to the Sun isn't the hottest.

title: Why Stars Twinkle but Planets Shine Steady
hook_line: Stars twinkle. Planets mostly shine steadily.
full_voiceover: Stars twinkle. Planets mostly shine steadily. The stars themselves aren't flickering. The twinkle happens in Earth's air, not in space. Our atmosphere is full of moving pockets of warmer and cooler air that bend light slightly as it passes through. A star is so far away that it's basically a single point of light, so every tiny bend makes it jump and flicker. Planets are much closer, so they appear as tiny disks. The flickers from different parts of the disk average out. That's a handy trick: if a bright dot shines steadily, there's a good chance it's a planet. Stars near the horizon twinkle most, because their light crosses more air. Astronauts above the air see steady stars. Have you used the twinkle test to find a planet? Tell me below.

title: Neptune Was Found With Math
hook_line: Neptune was predicted with math before it was spotted.
full_voiceover: Neptune was predicted with math before it was spotted. In the 1800s, astronomers noticed Uranus wasn't moving quite where its orbit said it should be. In 1846, he sent his prediction to the Berlin Observatory, and astronomers there found the planet the very first night they looked. It was within about one degree of the predicted spot, a tiny patch of sky. An English mathematician, John Couch Adams, had made similar calculations, and both are now often credited. title: Auroras Happen at Both Ends of the Earth
hook_line: Auroras happen at both ends of the Earth.
full_voiceover: Auroras happen at both ends of the Earth. Many people know the northern lights, but the southern lights are just as real, around the Antarctic region. They start with the Sun, which constantly sends out a stream of charged particles called the solar wind. Earth's magnetic field steers many of those particles toward the polar regions, where they slam into our upper atmosphere. When they hit oxygen and nitrogen, those gases glow. Oxygen often gives green, and sometimes red at higher altitudes. Nitrogen can add blue and purple tints, which is why the edges of some displays look violet.
